newsitem.title: USA: Palladium ends sharply higher, but NY gold lower.
newsitem.headline: Palladium ends sharply higher, but NY gold lower.

text.p: Platinum and palladium prices ended sharply higher Wednesday, as the five-month absence of Russian supplies resulted in an acute shortage of the white metals, but gold and silver ended lower with the uncertainty created by the dispute between the German government and Bundesbank now resolved.

"Russian supplies of platinum group metals are expected to resume in late June, but the backwardations suggest sharply lower prices later in the year, so fabricators and dealers are borrowing the metal in the meantime, pushing lease rates sky high," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.

Spot palladium soared about $35 an ounce Wednesday to around $233.00 an ounce, its highest levels in about 17 years, after fixing at $210 an ounce in London, its highest level since fixings began in 1989.
Short term one month lease rates for palladium rocketed to around 150 percent, from 75 percent Tuesday.
In the futures market, NYMEX June palladium ended up $21.15 an ounce at $202.80 an ounce. June palladium is now in its delivery period, ahead of its expiry on June 25.
The more-active NYMEX September palladium contract ended up $3.15 an ounce at $172.80.

NYMEX July platinum ended up $9.90 at $411.60 an ounce, while one month platinum lease rates rose to around 50 percent from 40 percent Tuesday. Earlier platinum fixed at $425.00 an ounce in London, its highest since February 7, 1996.
The other main metal in the platinum metals group, rhodium, jumped to around $330 an ounce Wednesday, from $275 Tuesday.
"Buying of rhodium by the Japanese suggested the talks over Russian export supplies may not be going too well," one PGM dealer said.

In overnight news, Russian officials told Japanese traders Russian exports would resume on June 20, after a five months suspension, but they also said the export licences had still not yet been granted by the Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations, suggesting further delays were possible.

Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and about 20 percent of its platinum. The U.S. recently replaced Japan has the largest user of palladium, which is used in automotive catalytic converter and in computer manufacturing.
Meanwhile, the deliveries of the NYMEX June palladium contract look to be proceeding without too many difficulties, analysts said.
NYMEX warehouse stocks of palladium were unchanged at 55,300 ounces Tuesday, while open interest in June palladium fell 138 lots to 761 contracts, or about 76,100 ounces.
But bullion bank, refining, and hedge fund sources said the shortage of metal in the physical market was so acute that defaults were a distinct possibility in the near future.
Already difficulties have been noted on one spot platinum transactions, while a trade house is believed to have suffered multi-million dollar losses on short positions, traders said.

"The Russians may start shipping in late June, but they have indicated they have indicated they will export at probably less than the same monthly rate as last year, say around eight tonnes a month (257,000 ounces), which means it may take a while to refill the Zurich vaults," one fund manager said.

"Given the Russian's shipped about their exports last year from stockpile and given a multimillion ounce leasebook which is masking demand, its possible the palladium/supply demand balance is actually in deficit," he said.

Meanwhile, COMEX August gold ended down $2.10 an ounce at $2.10 an ounce, with spot gold in the bullion market ending quoted $341.00/50, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $341.75 and the New York close Tuesday around $343.50/00.

COMEX July silver closed down 2.80 cents at $4.700 an ounce. The July/December contango ended around 10.4 cents, after narrowing recently from around 12.5 cents, amid talk a trade house was unwinding a short July 1997/long July 2001 position.

In the physical market, silver implied lease rates remained higher than normal around 3.80 percent for one month, after talk in the past few days of a player looking to borrow about 50 million ounces of silver.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1640))
